title: InterveneBench aggregate behavioral-simulator evaluation evidence

facts.statement: The headline evidence is a noncanonical prospective confirmation panel of six independent randomized experiments, five of which have bounded normalized decision utility.
Exactly 1,404 of 1,464 planned model outputs were strictly schema-valid; the 60 unavailable outputs were preserved without semantic repair or rerun.
The frozen primary simulator selected the exact sample-best intervention in 3 of 6 prospective experiments.
The probability that uniform random action selection would meet or exceed the observed exact-choice count is 0.3734567901234568, so exact-choice accuracy is chance-compatible.
Across the five normalized tasks, primary mean normalized regret is 0.003520577798391078 and worst normalized regret is 0.008544627721005615.
Uniform random action selection has mean normalized regret 0.040958979015419957; the primary-minus-uniform mean difference is -0.03743840121702888.
Only 12 of 216 complete uniform-random action combinations achieved mean regret as low as the primary policy, for a finite-action tail probability of 0.05555555555555555.
All 6 of 6 prospective choices satisfied their frozen task-specific practical-reliability rule.
The prespecified trust ranking was worse than random abstention: discrete AURC was 0.7111111111111111 versus a random-abstention expectation of 0.5, and exact-choice AUROC was 0.2222222222222222.
No prospectively validated trust threshold exists, and no confidence-based abstention policy is authorized.
No tested limited-human policy improved point regret over synthetic-only at any nonzero budget; human-only point estimates were worse at every tested nonzero budget.
Human-only pilots were resolved as worse at the 95 percent level for budgets 10, 25, 50, and 100.

Across 15 balanced empirical-Bayes task-by-budget cells, six updates were harmful, three corrective, and six unchanged; average harm was 13.59010662821557 times average correction, an exploratory pattern rather than a proven causal mechanism.
The Mistral cross-family comparison is retrospective and post-reveal, covers five experiments, and adds zero prospective experiment N.
On the five-task retrospective comparison, both the primary model and Mistral selected 40 percent of exact winners.
Mistral treatment-effect MAE was 0.050255692268200404 versus 0.06370846108314762 for the primary, while Mistral mean regret was 0.004295147420206114 versus 0.003520577798391078 for the primary.
The nine-experiment development set produced 8 of 9 exact choices and mean normalized regret 0.002316616844669365, but it is method-development evidence and not held-out confirmation.

reasons: uniform-action regret gate is not established
schema-validity rate is below autonomous threshold
trust ranking did not beat random abstention
tested limited-human fallback did not improve decisions

claim_boundaries.claim: a prospective low-regret signal on this six-experiment panel
a prospectively replicated negative result for the tested fallback family
a canonical benchmark or calibrated trust model

required_disclosures: The prospective panel is small and noncanonical: six experiments, five with bounded normalized utility.
Outcome-blind means target human outcomes were excluded before recommendation freeze; it does not prove absence from foundation-model pretraining.
The Mistral comparison was performed after outcomes were revealed and is architecture-sensitivity evidence, not prospective confirmation.
